module_title: Ratio Decidendi, Obiter Dicta, and Delegated Legislation
introduction: This intermediate tier dissects the anatomy of a judicial judgment, exploring exactly which part of a judge's ruling is legally binding. It also explores the hierarchy of legislation and how the Parliament outsources law-making power to the Executive.

core_concepts.title: Ratio Decidendi (The Reason for the Decision)
core_concepts.description:
Not every word a judge writes in a 500-page judgment is binding law.
- Meaning: The *Ratio Decidendi* is the underlying legal principle, rule, or core reasoning that directly determines the outcome of the case.
- Status: It is strictly **Authoritative and Binding** on lower courts. This is the actual 'Precedent'.

core_concepts.title: Obiter Dicta (Things Said by the Way)
core_concepts.description:
Meaning: These are casual remarks, hypothetical examples, or general observations made by a judge that are NOT strictly necessary to decide the case at hand.
- Status: Obiter Dicta is **Persuasive, not Binding**. Lower courts may respect it, but they are not legally forced to follow it.

core_concepts.title: Supreme vs. Subordinate Legislation
core_concepts.description:
- Supreme Legislation: Laws made directly by the sovereign authority of the State (e.g., Acts passed by the Parliament of India). It cannot be struck down by anyone except on constitutional grounds.
- Subordinate Legislation: Laws made by any other authority strictly under powers delegated by the Supreme Legislature. It is subordinate because it can be repealed or struck down by the Supreme Legislature or the Courts.

core_concepts.title: Delegated Legislation
core_concepts.description:
A specific type of Subordinate Legislation. Parliament passes a 'Parent Act' with a broad skeleton of laws, and 'delegates' the power to fill in the complex, technical details (Rules, Regulations, Bye-laws) to the Executive (Ministers/Bureaucrats).
- Why? Parliament lacks the time, technical expertise, and flexibility to write every single minute detail of modern administration.

important_entities.name: Per Incuriam
important_entities.significance: A highly tested exception to *Stare Decisis*. If a High Court or Supreme Court passes a judgment in ignorance of a relevant binding statute or a prior binding precedent, that decision is said to be *per incuriam*. Such decisions have **NO binding force** and do not act as valid precedents.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Can Parliament delegate all its power to the Executive? **NO**. The Supreme Court (in cases like *In re Delhi Laws Act*) has ruled that Parliament CANNOT delegate its 'Essential Legislative Function' (the power to declare the core policy of the law). It can only delegate ancillary/filling-in-the-blanks power.

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Use this quick association to separate the legally enforceable core of a judgment from the judge's casual commentary.

exam_strategy_tips: If a Judiciary question asks 'What is the legal status of an observation made by a Supreme Court judge based on a hypothetical scenario?', select **Obiter Dicta (Persuasive only)**.
